name: Ivan Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group that isn't tied to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a family firm, Hale and Son, three vans, mostly call-outs for letting agents and landlords. A normal day is five or six jobs: a tripping fuse box in a student house, a dead cooker point, a smoke alarm chirping in a flat above a chip shop. Old Mr Hale gives me the list on a printed sheet at eight, and I like that, I don't have to look at an app. I'm still learning, honestly, and if it gets complicated I ring his son Martin.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that every day's different and nobody's breathing down my neck. I don't like tenants who blame you for the landlord's mess, or parking. My grandmother left me a little one-bed which I rent out, so between that and my wages, my partner Grace and I are fine. We've got about nine months saved, maybe more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say not much, to be honest. I'm not online much. At work I'd just say it never affected us anyway, we fix fuse boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. I never wanted to learn any of it. Nobody was ever going to send a robot to a student house to find out why the fuse box keeps tripping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Finish my licence, keep doing the calls. Keep the flat rented to the same tenant if she stays. Maybe save toward a second flat in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal. Like a Monday that's just a Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at all that bothers you about the way things are now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My exam, a bit. I failed the theory part once already. And Mr Hale's 66, so I sometimes wonder what happens when he packs it in, whether Martin keeps the firm going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Mr Hale retired?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay with Martin if he carries on. If not, there are plenty of firms round here wanting juniors, I'd just ring around. I'm not worried about that.

say: I'd say **not much**, since I'm hardly online.
At work I'd say it **never affected** a firm that fixes fuse boxes.
think: I'm **glad**, because I never wanted to learn any of it.
No robot would get sent to find a **tripping fuse box** in a student house.
do: Finish my **licence** and keep doing the calls.
Keep the **inherited flat** rented to the same tenant.
Save toward a **second flat** in a few years.
S0.quote: Nobody was ever going to send a robot to a student house to find out why the fuse box keeps tripping.
fieldNote: Quiet, practical and **content**; the AI story barely touches his day.
His only worries are a **failed theory exam** and his boss retiring.
The **rental flat** gives him unusual security for a junior.

steps.text: Resit the licence theory exam this year
Save toward buying a second rental flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mainly an office thing, it doesn't touch us much. To friends I'd say people should learn what they need and not get too worked up. I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd worry the letting agents switch to some big app that sends the jobs to whoever's cheapest. Mr Hale gets his work through phone calls and knowing people. If letting agents book electricians through an app, a little firm like Hale and Son could lose half its calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep my head down. Maybe ask Martin if the firm needs to get on those apps, though I'd rather he dealt with it. Keep the flat and the savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. My own hands are still needed, but the work might come in a different way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the app side yourself if Martin asked you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If he asked, I'd do it, but I'd be slow and I'd moan. My partner Grace says I'm like her dad, who still writes cheques. She's not wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Hale, honestly. He does all the quoting in a notebook and knows every agent by first name. If they want an app instead, he'd find that hard, and he'd probably just retire.

say: I'd say it's an **office thing** that barely touches us.
I'd tell friends to learn what they need and **not get worked up**.
think: Letting agents might book through a **cheapest-wins app**.
A small firm like ours could **lose half** its calls.
do: **Keep working** and keep my head down.
Ask Martin whether the firm needs to get on **booking apps**.
Leave the **flat and savings** where they are.
feel: **Uneasy**, because the work might arrive differently.
S1.quote: If letting agents book electricians through an app, a little firm like Hale and Son could lose half its calls.
fieldNote: He sees risk through the **firm's sales channel**, not his tools.
Would learn apps only **if told to**, and admits he'd moan.

steps.text: Keep doing the daily call-outs for Hale and Son
Ask Martin whether the firm should join the booking apps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to slow it down a bit and look after people. I'm not one for marches, but I'd vote for whoever had a sensible plan. At work, I'd say let's see what actually happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be worried, yeah. The office side goes first, so Hale and Son's quoting and booking change in 2028. Then robots around 2031, when I'm 32. By the time robots can fix a fuse box, I'll be 32 and I'll never have learned anything else. At least I have the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my licence done and do as many calls as I could while they're there. I'd stop spending on the car upgrade and save harder, maybe double. I'd think about buying a second flat while I still have a wage to get a mortgage. I wouldn't go near the AI stuff unless I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, I've got the flat. But I'd feel like the ground is moving and I'm standing still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy a second flat. Isn't that a risk if lots of people lose jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If tenants can't pay, that's a problem. But I don't trust shares and I don't know what else to do with money. A flat's a flat, people still need somewhere to live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk to Grace about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's a dental nurse, she'd probably be fine longer than me. I'd tell my partner Grace we'd be all right with the rent coming in, and I'd mean it, mostly. We'd put off the wedding money for a year, maybe.

say: I'd say the government should **slow it down** and look after people.
I'd **vote** for whoever had a sensible plan.
think: Robots could fix fuse boxes by **2031**, when I'm 32.
At least the **rental flat** gives me something.
do: Do as many **calls** as possible while they last.
Skip the **car upgrade** and double my saving.
Buy a **second flat** while I still have a wage for a mortgage.
feel: **Anxious**, like the ground moves while I stand still.
S2.quote: By the time robots can fix a fuse box, I'll be 32 and I'll never have learned anything else.
fieldNote: Expects his **trade work to shrink** within about five years and won't retrain.
His hedge is **property**, the only investment he trusts.
Would delay the **wedding** fund rather than change careers.

steps.text: Cancel the car upgrade and double monthly saving
Buy a second rental flat while still earning
Delay the wedding savings for a year
Vote for the party with a sensible AI plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same thing, really. The government should plan for it, there's time. At work I'd tell the lads not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years to the thinking AI and robots by 2034 is more manageable. I'd be 35. I could build up the rental side so it covers our basics. If I can get two flats paid down by 35, a robot taking my job won't take our home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get licensed, keep working hard. Buy the second flat in a couple of years. Keep my savings in cash. I'd probably not learn the new stuff until Martin made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's time to sort something, and I like having time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you won't learn the new tools. What if Martin does make you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do it, slowly. I'm not stupid, I just don't like it. Grace would help me, she's better with phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lads who are just starting, the 18-year-olds. They're going into a trade that might be done by the time they're any good. Somebody should tell them straight.

say: I'd say the government has **time to plan** for it properly.
I'd tell the younger lads at work **not to panic** yet.
think: Robots arriving by **2034**, when I'm 35, feels more manageable to me.
Two **paid-down flats** would protect our home even if my job went.
do: Buy the **second flat** in a couple of years.
S3.quote: If I can get two flats paid down by 35, a robot taking my job won't take our home.
fieldNote: Extra time lets him lean on his **property plan**, easing his mood.
Concern for **new apprentices** shows quiet empathy.

steps.text: Buy a second rental flat within two years
Keep working calls for Hale and Son

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, plenty can change. At work I'd shrug, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think I'm fine. Robots in 2039, I'd be 40, with two flats and maybe Hale and Son if Martin wanted a partner. Ten years is long enough for me to stop needing the wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same plan, slower. Licence, second flat, maybe a third by 38. Keep doing the calls. Probably still no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the edges, but mostly calm. It feels far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd still be an electrician in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe part-time, doing the jobs people want a person for. Old ladies who want someone they know to come round. I could see myself doing that and living off the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd change now, knowing this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably pass that theory exam first time. Grace says I should take a course on landlord stuff too, like tax. I might, if it's not online.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long time** and plenty can change.
At work I'd just **shrug** about it.
think: By **2039** I'd be 40, with two flats and maybe a share in the firm.
I might **not need** the wage by the time robots arrive.
do: Stick with the **licence** and second-flat plan.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for me to stop needing the wage.
fieldNote: His answer to AI is to slowly become a **landlord** with a trade on the side.
Small **edge of worry** remains because his skills stay narrow.

steps.text: Buy a third rental flat by age 38
Take an in-person course on landlord tax
Keep doing call-outs part-time for regular customers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be 32 with nothing else I know how to do. What'd help is time, really, and maybe some sensible training that's in person, not on an app. I'm not against progress, I just want someone to explain it to me face to face.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Maybe ask people what they've got to fall back on. My nan's flat changes everything for me, and most lads my age don't have that.

headlineQuote: I'm not against progress, I just want someone to explain it to me face to face.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old junior** at a small call-out firm, with an inherited **rental flat**.
He avoids AI and apps and prefers **printed job sheets**.
His answer to every AGI picture is to build up **property** rather than retrain.
He's anxious only in AGI by 2028, and **uneasy** when there's more time.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd be **32** with no other skills.
whatWouldHelp: More **time**, and **in-person** training rather than apps.
